ai.definition: Femtotechnology refers to the theoretical engineering at a scale of 10^-15 meters, focusing on manipulating the internal structure of atomic nuclei. This involves directly altering quarks and gluons within nucleons.
ai.howItWorks: Theoretically, femtotechnological processes would use high-energy density focal points to precisely rearrange the quarks and gluons that make up nucleons (the protons and neutrons in atomic nuclei).
ai.problemSolved: Femtotechnology aims to address challenges such as ultra-dense energy storage and creating exotic materials like neutronium alloys, which could revolutionize energy density and material properties.
ai.manufacturing: Current theoretical frameworks suggest that manufacturing at this scale would require extremely precise control over high-energy fields. However, the technology is currently purely speculative and no practical methods exist for achieving femtotechnological manipulation.
ai.buildProcess: The build process remains undefined due to the current stage of theory. It's hypothesized that it might involve advanced particle accelerators or similar devices capable of generating the necessary energy densities.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers are not well-defined but would likely include the extreme precision and energy requirements needed for such processes, as well as the development of new technologies to achieve femtotechnological manipulation.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The field is in its infancy with no practical applications or prototypes. Theoretical research may continue indefinitely without immediate commercial viability.
ai.regulation: Currently, there are no specific regulations for femtotechnology as it remains purely theoretical and unproven. However, if developed, regulatory frameworks would likely be necessary to address potential safety concerns and ethical implications.
ai.risks: Theoretical risks include the possibility of unintended consequences from manipulating atomic nuclei, such as creating unstable isotopes or other dangerous particles. There are also significant technical challenges in achieving the required energy densities and precision.
ai.profitability: Profitability is not currently possible given the purely theoretical nature of femtotechnology. However, if developed, it could lead to revolutionary applications that might significantly impact various industries, potentially leading to high profitability down the line.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development would require significant advancements in particle physics and materials science. Theoretical research into quantum mechanics and nuclear physics is ongoing but has not yet led to practical femtotechnological capabilities.
ai.energyRequirements: Operational power draw for field units could be in the low hundreds of watts, though this is speculative. Manufacturing energy intensity would be extremely high due to the need for precise control over high-energy fields, potentially requiring megawatts or more of energy input during fabrication processes.

glossary.def: Engineering at the scale of 10^-15 meters, focusing on manipulating atomic nuclei.
Theoretical devices that could generate extremely high energy densities for precise manipulation of subatomic particles.
Subatomic particles that make up protons and neutrons within atomic nuclei.
Protons and neutrons, the building blocks of atomic nuclei.

subsystems.name: Energy driver
subsystems.role: delivers energies of millions to billions of electronvolts — the scale of nuclear, not atomic, binding.

subsystems.name: Target and trap
subsystems.role: holds a single nucleus or a small sample long enough for a controlled change.

subsystems.name: Nucleus-modifying stage
subsystems.role: changes the number of protons and neutrons, or raises nuclei into long-lived excited states.

subsystems.name: Diagnostics
subsystems.role: detects what happens at the 10^-15 m scale, which can never be seen directly.

subsystems.name: Containment and shielding
subsystems.role: manages radiation, heat and any unstable product.

subsystems.name: Energy conversion
subsystems.role: stabilises the engineered state and turns released energy into heat and electricity.

buildSteps.title: Reach the energy scale
buildSteps.detail: Accelerators and lasers already create quark–gluon plasma in collider experiments, but only as fleeting, uncontrolled fireballs. A practical route would need focused beams at nuclear-scale energy density, not bulk heating.

buildSteps.title: Isolate a target species
buildSteps.detail: Isotopes must be separated to high purity before any nuclear structure is altered, since ordinary material is a mixture of isotopes.

buildSteps.title: Transmute the nucleus
buildSteps.detail: Change proton or neutron number by neutron capture, charged-particle bombardment or photon-induced reactions — processes proven in reactors and accelerators, though at low efficiency and high energy cost.

buildSteps.title: Populate long-lived excited states
buildSteps.detail: Some nuclei can be driven into metastable 'isomer' states that hold energy for minutes to years (hafnium-178m2 is the classic example). The contested part is releasing that energy on demand, which has not been reliably demonstrated.

buildSteps.title: Assemble nuclear-scale structures
buildSteps.detail: Instead of chemical bonds, this would rely on the strong force. Matter bound this way — neutron-degenerate matter — exists naturally only inside neutron stars, where gravity supplies the confining pressure.

buildSteps.title: Contain the product
buildSteps.detail: No laboratory container can supply the pressures needed to hold neutron-rich matter stable. Any route would first require a containment method that does not yet exist in known physics.

buildSteps.title: Convert energy to electricity
buildSteps.detail: Released energy would appear as heat and radiation, needing shielding, heat exchangers and a turbine — a well-understood step once the source works at all.

buildSteps.title: Operate and control
buildSteps.detail: Timing and dose control at the nuclear level would decide whether this is a power source or an explosion; feedback systems would have to act on nuclear timescales.

prerequisites.why: they are the only tools that reach nuclear energy densities, though with very low wall-plug efficiency.
these already let us change nuclei, but slowly and at a large energy cost.
storing energy in excited nuclei is real; triggering its release on demand has not been reproduced reliably.
quarks are permanently confined inside nucleons, so rearranging them individually is not possible with any known method.
stable ultra-dense matter needs pressures comparable to a star's interior.

pathway.milestone: nuclear transmutation and isomer research in accelerators and reactors
pathway.unlocks: a catalogue of nuclei and excited states to work from.

pathway.milestone: a controllable nuclear-isomer energy store if the effect can be reproduced
pathway.unlocks: energy storage thousands of times denser than chemical batteries.

pathway.milestone: engineered isotopes for long-lived compact power sources
pathway.unlocks: niche uses such as deep-space probes, not grid power.

pathway.milestone: nuclear-scale assembly, if a containment route is ever found
pathway.unlocks: ultra-dense materials and energy storage — at present a theoretical limit, not an engineering programme.
